title: Audio embeddings and classification
summary: How pretrained audio networks turn log-mel patches into embeddings and multi-label scores, how to pool and evaluate them with mAP, and how AST, SpecAugment and CLAP extend them.
outcomes: Compute how many 0.96 s patches YAMNet produces for a clip and trace one patch to a 1024-d embedding
Explain why audio taggers use per-class sigmoids and when mean or max pooling of patch scores fails
Compute average precision and mAP for a small multi-label example
Choose between frozen embeddings, fine-tuning and CLAP zero-shot for a new sound task
Describe how AST tokenizes spectrograms and how SpecAugment masks time and frequency

lessons.title: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches

blocks.md:
Say you want a backyard device that notices barking, sirens or a particular bird. Training a sound classifier from scratch needs many thousands of labeled clips per class. The practical route is to borrow a network that was already trained on a huge labeled audio collection and reuse what it learned.

That collection is usually **AudioSet** (Gemmeke et al., ICASSP 2017): human-labeled 10-second clips from YouTube videos. The current release labels **527 sound classes** on about **2.1 million clips** (2,084,320 on the official page), drawn from a hierarchical ontology of 632 event categories such as Speech, Dog, Siren and Rain.

A pretrained audio model gives you two things for each short window of sound:

- an **embedding**: a fixed-size vector (128 numbers for VGGish, 1024 for YAMNet) that summarizes what the window sounds like, and
- **class scores**: one probability per AudioSet class.

This course follows that pipeline from raw samples to clip-level decisions, then shows how such models are evaluated (mAP), how transformers and augmentation improved them, and how text embeddings (CLAP) let you classify with labels you only type at test time.

From the signal processing prerequisite, recall that a **short-time Fourier transform (STFT)** slides a window along the signal and takes a spectrum at each step, giving a time by frequency picture. Google's VGGish and YAMNet use nearly the same front end, documented in the YAMNet README:

1. Resample to **16 kHz mono**.
2. STFT magnitudes with a **25 ms** periodic Hann window every **10 ms**.
3. Map to **64 mel bins** covering 125 to 7500 Hz (mel bins are wider at high frequencies, roughly matching pitch perception).
4. Take $\log(\text{mel} + 0.001)$; the offset avoids $\log 0$ (the VGGish README gives 0.01).
5. Cut the result into **patches of 96 frames x 64 bins**, that is 0.96 s each (YAMNet overlaps them by 50%; VGGish patches do not overlap).

blocks.title: YAMNet front end and model, one patch at a time

scenes.caption: Audio is resampled to 16 kHz mono first. The model was trained on exactly this feature pipeline, so any other rate or channel layout must be converted.
The STFT gives one spectrum every 10 ms from a 25 ms window, then a mel filterbank squeezes it to 64 bands and a log compresses the huge dynamic range.
96 consecutive 10 ms frames form one 96 x 64 patch, the unit the network sees: 0.96 s of sound.
MobileNet v1 turns the patch into a 3 x 2 grid of 1024 activations; averaging the grid gives the 1024-d embedding.
A single logistic layer maps the embedding to 521 independent sigmoid scores, one per class. The network part runs once for every patch in the clip.

blocks.prompt: YAMNet's patches are 0.96 s long and start every 0.48 s (50% overlap). How many patches, and so how many rows of scores, does it produce for a 5.0 s clip?
blocks.reveal: **10.** YAMNet first zero-pads the waveform so it covers a whole number of hops. A 5 s clip is 80,000 samples; `pad_waveform` grows it to 84,720 samples (5.295 s). That gives 528 STFT frames, and $1 + \lfloor (528 - 96)/48 \rfloor = 10$ patches. Our script re-implements the padding rule from the YAMNet source to get these numbers.

blocks.title: Ten overlapping 0.96 s patches cover a 5 s clip

scenes.caption: Patch 0 covers 0 to 0.96 s. One row of 521 scores and one 1024-d embedding come out of it.
Patch 1 starts 0.48 s later, so every moment after the first 0.48 s (until the last patch's final 0.48 s) is seen by two patches.
Hopping by 0.48 s continues. Overlap means a short event is less likely to be cut in half at a patch boundary.
Patch 9 runs from 4.32 to 5.28 s, past the end of the clip: its tail is the zero padding. Total: 10 patches, so the scores matrix has shape (10, 521).

blocks.md: Clip length does not map to patches by simple division. YAMNet needs at least 0.975 s of audio (0.96 s plus the rest of the last 25 ms STFT window), pads anything shorter with silence, and rounds longer audio up to a whole hop. Our script gets 1 patch for 0.5 s, **2 patches for 1.0 s**, 10 for 5 s and 20 for 10 s.

A pretrained audio model never sees a whole clip at once. It sees fixed 0.96 s log-mel patches and returns one embedding and one score vector per patch. Everything about clip-level decisions (lesson 3) is about combining those per-patch outputs.

blocks.question: Using the same padding rule, how many YAMNet patches (score rows) does a 10.0 s clip produce?
options: 10, one per second
21, because the last partial hop adds an extra patch
blocks.explain: The 10 s clip is padded to 161,520 samples, giving 1008 STFT frames and $1 + \lfloor (1008 - 96)/48 \rfloor = 20$ patches. Twenty patches at a 0.48 s hop span 0 to 10.08 s.

blocks.question: Your microphone records 44.1 kHz stereo. What should happen before the audio reaches YAMNet?
options: Nothing: a CNN is invariant to sample rate
Keep 44.1 kHz but use only the left channel
Convert to mono and resample to 16 kHz, because the mel bins and patch timing were fixed during training
Resample to 8 kHz to save compute; the 125 to 7500 Hz band still fits
blocks.explain: The model learned weights for a specific feature pipeline: 16 kHz mono, 25 ms / 10 ms STFT, 64 mel bins from 125 to 7500 Hz. At 8 kHz the Nyquist frequency is 4 kHz, so the bins above it would be empty, and at 44.1 kHz the frame and bin layout would no longer match what the weights expect.

lessons.title: Embeddings as features: VGGish, YAMNet and PANNs

blocks.md: An **embedding** is the activation vector just before the classification layer. From the representation learning prerequisite: training on a large labeled task forces this vector to encode what separates the classes, so nearby vectors tend to mean similar sounds. You can then train a tiny model on top for your own classes.

Three widely used families:

- **VGGish** (from Hershey et al. 2017, *CNN Architectures for Large-Scale Audio Classification*): a VGG variant from that paper's architecture comparison on 70M YouTube videos with video-level labels (the comparison used a 3K subset of the 30,871 labels; the README says the released model was trained on a preliminary version of YouTube-8M). Its last layer is a **128-wide** fully connected embedding on each 0.96 s, 96 x 64 log-mel patch. The embedding is pre-activation, and the AudioSet release also PCA-whitened and 8-bit quantized it.
- **YAMNet**: MobileNet v1 on the same patches, a **1024-d** embedding, 521 AudioSet classes (527 minus six dropped on fairness review), 3.7M weights and 69.2M multiplies per patch, small by modern standards.
- **PANNs** (Kong et al. 2020): CNNs trained on all of AudioSet at 32 kHz. The CNN14 model has a **2048-d** embedding and reaches **0.431 mAP** on AudioSet tagging.

PANNs compared three ways to reuse a pretrained network on a new task:

1. **Frozen embedding + new head**: compute embeddings once, train only a small classifier on them.
2. **Fine-tune**: start from the pretrained weights and update all of them on the new data.
3. **Train from scratch** as the baseline.

The test bed was **ESC-50** (Piczak 2015): 2,000 five-second environmental recordings, 50 classes with 40 clips each, pre-split into 5 folds so that fragments of the same source recording stay in one fold.

blocks.title: Two ways to reuse a pretrained audio network

scenes.caption: Inference path: the pretrained network turns the clip into an embedding, and a head trained for your classes reads it.
Frozen mode: only the head learns. Embeddings can be computed once and cached, so training is cheap and works with little data.
Fine-tune mode: gradients also flow into the backbone. It adapts features to your domain but costs a full forward and backward pass per clip and can overfit small datasets.

blocks.title: ESC-50 accuracy with and without AudioSet pretraining (PANNs)

scenes.caption: Training CNN14 from scratch on ESC-50 alone reaches 0.833 accuracy (PANNs paper, Table XIII).
Freezing the AudioSet-pretrained CNN14 and training only new layers on top already beats scratch: 0.908 with one layer, 0.918 with three.
Fine-tuning everything is best at 0.947. Simplified: these are single numbers from one paper and setup; the ranking can change with very small or very different datasets.

blocks.code:
import tensorflow as tf, tensorflow_hub as hub

yamnet = hub.load('https://tfhub.dev/google/yamnet/1')

def embed(wav_16k_mono):
    # scores: (n_patches, 521), embeddings: (n_patches, 1024)
    scores, embeddings, log_mel = yamnet(wav_16k_mono)
    return embeddings

# small head trained on frozen YAMNet embeddings
head = tf.keras.Sequential([
    tf.keras.layers.Input(shape=(1024,)),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(512, activation='relu'),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(num_classes),
])
blocks.caption: Frozen-embedding transfer, following the TensorFlow tutorial on YAMNet with ESC-50. Each patch embedding becomes one training example carrying its clip's label.

blocks.md: Split by clip (or by source recording), never by patch. Patches of one clip overlap by 50% and share the same label, so a random patch-level split puts near-copies in train and test and inflates accuracy. ESC-50 ships 5 folds for this reason, and the TensorFlow tutorial carries each clip's fold number along with every patch embedding and splits by fold.

blocks.question: You have 300 labeled 5 s clips for 6 classes and a laptop CPU. What is the most sensible first model?
options: Train a CNN from scratch on log-mel spectrograms
Cache YAMNet (or PANNs) embeddings once and train a small head on them
Fine-tune a full AST transformer end to end
Skip pretrained models and use raw waveform samples as features with logistic regression
blocks.explain: With a few hundred clips, a frozen pretrained backbone plus a small head is cheap to train and usually strong, as the PANNs ESC-50 numbers suggest. Fine-tuning can add accuracy later if you have the compute and enough data; scratch training starts far behind.

blocks.question: A teammate reports 99% test accuracy after shuffling all patch embeddings from 300 clips and splitting 80/20. What is the most likely explanation?
options: YAMNet embeddings are simply very good for this task
Leakage: overlapping patches of the same clip landed in both train and test
The head is too small to overfit
Sigmoid outputs inflate accuracy compared with softmax
blocks.explain: Each 5 s clip yields 10 patches that overlap by half and share one label. A patch-level shuffle lets the model match test patches to near-identical training patches. Split by clip or source recording first, then expand to patches.

lessons.title: Sigmoid outputs and pooling patch scores into a clip score

blocks.md: Real recordings contain several sounds at once. In AudioSet each 10 s segment carries on average **2.7 labels**, and Music appears in 56% of segments (Gemmeke et al.). So audio tagging is **multi-label**: a clip can be Dog *and* Speech *and* Vehicle.

A softmax output makes classes compete: the probabilities sum to 1, so raising Dog must lower Speech. Audio taggers instead put a **sigmoid** on each class score independently, so each output is its own yes/no probability. YAMNet's classifier activation is `sigmoid`, and PANNs, AST and the Hershey et al. CNNs are all trained with per-class sigmoid outputs and **binary cross-entropy**:

blocks.caption: Binary cross-entropy summed over clips n and classes k, as written in the PANNs paper. Each class is a separate binary problem; $y_{nk} \in \{0,1\}$.

blocks.md:
There is a second mismatch. Labels describe a whole clip ("a dog barks somewhere in these 10 s"), but frame-based models like YAMNet score each 0.96 s patch. Such clip-level labels are called **weak labels**. When Hershey et al. trained on video labels, each 960 ms frame simply inherited all labels of its video. At inference you need the reverse: **pool** the per-patch scores into one clip score per class.

YAMNet's `inference.py` and the TF Hub tutorial use the **mean** over patches; the TensorFlow transfer tutorial notes that mean or **max** aggregation both work. Which is better depends on how long the sound lasts.

blocks.prompt: A 5 s clip (10 patches) contains one short dog bark, captured in patches 4 and 5 with Dog scores 0.92 and 0.85. Every other patch scores about 0.02 to 0.05. With a 0.5 threshold, does mean pooling detect the dog? Does max pooling?
blocks.reveal: Mean pooling gives **0.203**, below 0.5, so the bark is missed: eight quiet patches dilute two loud ones. Max pooling gives **0.92** and detects it. Short, sparse events are exactly where mean pooling fails.

blocks.title: Mean vs max pooling over 10 patch scores (toy numbers)

scenes.caption: Toy per-patch Dog scores for a 5 s clip with one bark in patches 4 and 5.
Mean pooling: (0.02 + 0.03 + ... + 0.03) / 10 = 0.203. Below 0.5, so the clip is tagged as no dog.
Max pooling picks the single loudest patch, 0.92. The bark is detected.
A sustained sound behaves differently. Rain scores near 0.6 in every patch: mean 0.60, max 0.65. Both pooling rules agree.
The cost of max: one glitchy patch scoring 0.71 for Siren in a quiet clip. Max says 0.71 (false alarm); mean says 0.11 (correctly no siren).

blocks.md: Mean pooling suits sounds that last (rain, engine hum, music) and resists one-patch glitches. Max pooling catches short events (a bark, a door slam, a gunshot) but turns any single false patch into a clip-level false alarm. PANNs combines both inside the network: its global pooling sums the time-averaged and the time-maximized feature vectors.

Do not apply softmax across AudioSet classes and then threshold. A clip with dog and speech would have to split probability between them. Use the model's per-class sigmoid scores, and tune a threshold per class if you need hard yes/no tags.

blocks.question: A noise monitor must flag rare glass-break sounds lasting under half a second in 10 s clips. Missed events are costly; occasional false alarms are reviewed by a person. Which clip-level rule fits best?
options: Max over patch scores, with a per-class threshold tuned on validation clips
Mean over patch scores with a 0.5 threshold
Softmax over the 521 classes, then argmax
Use only the first patch of each clip to save compute
blocks.explain: A sub-second event fills one or two of the 20 patches, so mean pooling dilutes it. Max keeps it, and a tuned threshold controls the false alarm rate. Argmax would also hide glass breaking whenever louder speech or music is present.

blocks.question: A clip contains a barking dog and a person talking. Model A uses softmax over classes; model B uses independent sigmoids. Which statement is correct?
options: Both can output 0.9 for Dog and 0.9 for Speech
Only model A can output high scores for both
Only model B can output 0.9 for Dog and 0.9 for Speech at the same time
Neither can; multi-label clips need two separate models
blocks.explain: Softmax outputs sum to 1, so two classes cannot both be 0.9. Independent sigmoids treat each class as its own binary question, which is why audio taggers trained on AudioSet use sigmoid outputs and binary cross-entropy.

lessons.title: Scoring a tagger: average precision and mAP

blocks.md:
How do you score a model that outputs 527 probabilities per clip? Accuracy at a fixed threshold is a poor fit: most classes are rare, so predicting "absent" everywhere looks accurate, and the best threshold differs per class.

AudioSet papers instead use **mean average precision (mAP)**. For each class separately, rank all evaluation clips by that class's score. **Average precision (AP)** looks at the ranking only, not at any threshold. **mAP** is the mean of AP over classes.

Hershey et al. define AP as the precision "averaged across lists just long enough to include each individual positive". In symbols: walk down the ranked list; each time you reach a true positive at rank $r$, record the precision $P@r$ (positives so far divided by $r$); average those values over the $R$ positives.

blocks.tex: \mathrm{AP}_k = \frac{1}{R_k} \sum_{r:\, \text{clip at rank } r \text{ is positive}} P@r, \qquad \mathrm{mAP} = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathrm{AP}_k
blocks.caption: For class k with R_k positive clips. This matches scikit-learn average_precision_score when scores have no ties.

scenes.caption: Sigmoid scores from a hypothetical tagger on six clips. Each column will be ranked on its own.
Highlighted cells are the true labels. The task is multi-label: c1 has Dog and Speech, c2 has Rain and Speech.
Note c4 scores 0.75 for Speech but contains no speech, and c3 scores 0.65 for Dog without a dog. These errors will lower AP.

blocks.title: Ranking each class and reading off precision at each hit

scenes.caption: Rain: c2 and c3 are hits at ranks 1 and 2 (P = 1, 1), c5 is a miss, c6 a hit at rank 4 (P = 3/4). AP = 0.917.
Averaging the three APs gives mAP = 0.852. Our script checks this against scikit-learn's average_precision_score (macro average).

blocks.md: AP depends on how common a class is: a random ranking gets an AP near the class's positive rate. Hershey et al. note that most of their classes had priors below $10^{-4}$, so reported mAPs look small even when false alarm rates are good. Only compare mAP numbers computed on the same evaluation set and class list.

Reference points on AudioSet, each from its own paper:

- AudioSet paper baseline (485 classes at the time): balanced mAP 0.314.
- YAMNet README (521 classes, 20,366-segment eval set): balanced mAP 0.306.
- PANNs CNN14: 0.431.
- AST (lesson 5): 0.459 for the best single model, 0.485 for an ensemble.

The setups differ (class lists, eval set versions, balancing), so treat these as rough landmarks rather than a leaderboard.

blocks.question: For one class, the ranked list of 4 clips is: positive, negative, negative, positive. What is the AP?
blocks.explain: The hits are at ranks 1 and 4, with precision 1/1 = 1 and 2/4 = 0.5. Their mean is 0.75.

blocks.question: You raise the decision threshold for Dog from 0.5 to 0.8 without changing the model. What happens to Dog AP?
options: It is unchanged, because AP depends only on the ranking of scores
It rises, because fewer false positives are output
It falls, because fewer positives are detected
It becomes undefined
blocks.explain: AP is computed from the order of clips by score, sweeping every possible cut-off. A threshold only matters when you convert scores into hard tags for a product, which is a separate decision.

lessons.title: AST and SpecAugment: patches, attention and masked bands

blocks.md: CNNs such as VGGish, YAMNet and PANNs look at local time-frequency neighborhoods and grow their view layer by layer. The **Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST)** of Gong, Chung and Glass (2021) drops convolutions entirely: it treats the spectrogram like an image in a Vision Transformer, so every patch can attend to every other patch from the first layer.

AST's recipe, from the paper:

1. A $t$-second clip becomes **128** log-mel filterbank features every 10 ms (25 ms Hamming window): a $128 \times 100t$ spectrogram.
2. Cut it into **16 x 16 patches** that overlap by 6 in both time and frequency.
3. Project each patch to a 768-d vector, add a learned positional embedding, prepend a [CLS] token.
4. Run a standard Transformer encoder (12 layers, 12 heads, width 768).
5. A linear layer with **sigmoid** on the [CLS] output gives the class scores.

The weights start from an ImageNet-trained vision transformer (DeiT), which the paper shows helps noticeably, most of all when audio training data is small.

blocks.caption: Number of patches (sequence length) from the AST paper. The 12 is the number of patch rows across 128 mel bins with stride 10.

blocks.md: AST reached 0.459 mAP on AudioSet as a single model (0.485 as an ensemble) and 95.6% accuracy on ESC-50 when also pretrained on AudioSet (88.7% with ImageNet pretraining only). The price is sequence length: self-attention cost grows with the square of $N$, and a 10 s clip already gives 1188 tokens by the formula (the paper's Table 5 lists 1212 for its AudioSet model).

Both PANNs and AST train with **SpecAugment** (Park et al. 2019), originally proposed for speech recognition. It edits the log-mel spectrogram itself, treating it like an image:

- **Frequency masking**: choose a width $f$ uniformly from 0 to a parameter $F$, a start $f_0$ in $[0, \nu - f)$ where $\nu$ is the number of mel channels, and blank bins $f_0$ to $f_0 + f - 1$.
- **Time masking**: the same with width $t$ up to $T$ over consecutive time steps.
- An optional time warp, and several masks per example.

The spectrograms are normalized to zero mean, so setting masked values to 0 equals filling them with the mean.

blocks.title: SpecAugment on a toy 8 x 12 log-mel spectrogram

scenes.caption: Toy normalized log-mel spectrogram (mean about 0): a two-band tonal sound (mel 6 and mel 3) from t3 to t9, and a low-frequency thump at t0 and t1.
Frequency mask with f = 2, f0 = 5: rows mel 5 and mel 6 are set to 0 for every time step. One of the tone's two bands disappears.
Time mask instead, with t = 3, t0 = 5: steps t5 to t7 are set to 0 in every band. The tone now has a gap in the middle.
Both masks together. The label is still the same sound, so the model must recognize it from the remaining band and the remaining time steps.

blocks.prompt: Why would hiding parts of the input make a classifier better on clean test audio?
blocks.reveal: Masking removes the easy shortcut of relying on one band or one moment. The model has to use several partial cues, which is what it needs when real recordings have a band covered by wind noise or an event partly overlapped by another sound. It acts as a regularizer, and it costs almost nothing because it runs on features already in memory.

blocks.md: Scale the mask sizes to your input. SpecAugment's LibriSpeech basic policy used F = 27 mel channels and T = 100 time steps with one mask of each kind; AST used a maximum time mask of 192 frames and a maximum frequency mask of 48 bins on its 128-bin inputs. Copied unchanged to a 64-bin input, a 48-bin mask could hide three quarters of the spectrum.

blocks.question: Using AST's formula, how many patches does a 5 s clip produce?
blocks.explain: $100t - 16 = 484$, divided by 10 and rounded up gives 49 patch columns; times 12 rows gives 588. The 10 s case gives 1188.

blocks.question: A teammate implements frequency masking by writing -80 (very quiet in their dB scale) into masked bins of unnormalized log-mel features. What is the problem?
options: Nothing, silence is the most natural mask value
Masks must be applied to the waveform, not the spectrogram
Frequency masks must always cover exactly F bins
The masked block becomes an extreme, easy-to-spot value instead of the mean; SpecAugment normalizes to zero mean so 0 equals the mean
blocks.explain: In the paper, features are normalized to zero mean and masked values are set to 0, which is the mean. Filling with an extreme value creates an unnatural pattern the model can learn to detect, and it shifts the input statistics compared with test time.

lessons.title: Zero-shot classification with CLAP audio and text embeddings

blocks.md: Every model so far has a fixed label list. Adding a class (say, "leaf blower") needs labeled clips and retraining. **CLAP**, Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (Elizalde et al. 2022), removes that limit by putting audio and text in the **same embedding space**.

CLAP has two encoders, a CNN14 audio encoder (from PANNs) and a BERT text encoder, each followed by a learned projection to a shared 1024-d space. It was trained on about 128k audio-caption pairs with a contrastive loss: in a batch of $N$ pairs, the similarity matrix should be high on the $N$ matching pairs and low elsewhere. This is the same contrastive idea from the representation learning prerequisite, applied across two modalities.

**Zero-shot classification**, as the CLAP paper describes it:

1. Turn each class label into a sentence, for example "This is a sound of dog barking", and embed it with the text encoder.
2. Embed the audio clip with the audio encoder.
3. Compute the **cosine similarity** between the audio vector and each text vector.
4. Turn the similarities into probabilities with softmax (single-label tasks) or sigmoid (multi-label tasks).

No audio labels for these classes are ever used. CLAP reported 82.6% zero-shot accuracy on ESC-50.

blocks.title: CLAP zero-shot: one audio vector, one text vector per label

nodes.label:
This is a sound
of dog barking

scenes.caption: The audio encoder and its projection map the clip to one vector in the shared space.
Each candidate label is wrapped in a prompt sentence and embedded by the text encoder. The label list is chosen at test time.
Cosine similarity between the audio vector and each text vector gives one logit per label; the highest wins.

blocks.md: Here is the arithmetic with **illustrative 4-d toy vectors** (real CLAP vectors have 1024 dimensions and come from the trained encoders). Audio $a = (0.8, 0.1, 0.5, 0.2)$. Text vectors: dog barking $(0.7, 0.2, 0.6, 0.1)$, rain $(0.1, 0.9, 0.2, 0.3)$, car horn $(0.3, 0.1, 0.1, 0.9)$.

blocks.tex: \cos(a, b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{\lVert a \rVert \, \lVert b \rVert}, \qquad p_j = \frac{e^{s \cos(a, t_j)}}{\sum_i e^{s \cos(a, t_i)}}
blocks.caption: Cosine similarity, then a softmax with a scale s (the inverse of a temperature). CLAP learns this temperature during training.

blocks.prompt: The cosine similarities come out as 0.978 (dog barking), 0.349 (rain) and 0.516 (car horn). If you apply a plain softmax (scale 1), will the dog get a confident probability like 0.9?
blocks.reveal: No: only **0.462**. Cosines live in [-1, 1], so with scale 1 the logits differ by at most about 0.6 and the softmax stays flat (0.462, 0.246, 0.291). That is why contrastive models multiply similarities by a learned inverse temperature. With an illustrative scale of 10 the same cosines give 0.988, 0.002, 0.010. The ranking never changes, only the confidence.

blocks.title: Toy zero-shot scores for three labels (illustrative vectors)

scenes.caption: Cosine similarity of the toy audio vector with each prompt vector. Dog barking is closest.
Softmax with scale 1: the right answer wins but the distribution is nearly flat, because cosine values are bounded.
Softmax with scale 10 (illustrative): the same ranking, now confident. For multi-label tasks CLAP uses a sigmoid per label instead of a softmax.

blocks.md: Prompt wording matters. On ESC-50, CLAP's zero-shot accuracy ranged from 0.786 with "i can hear [class label]" to 0.826 with "this is a sound of [class label]". The paper attributes this to training captions being sentences while dataset labels are one or two words.

**LAION-CLAP** (Wu, Chen et al. 2022) scaled the idea up: it released LAION-Audio-630K (633,526 audio-text pairs), added feature fusion so the encoder handles variable-length audio, and used keyword-to-caption augmentation to turn bare labels into sentences. It reports state-of-the-art zero-shot classification and text-to-audio retrieval at the time of publication.

Choosing an approach: use a pretrained tagger's scores directly when AudioSet classes cover your needs; train a small head on frozen embeddings when you have a few hundred labeled clips; fine-tune when you have more data and compute; use CLAP-style zero-shot when labels change often or you have no labeled audio, and expect lower accuracy than a supervised head on the same classes.

blocks.question: A wildlife app must add new insect sound categories every week, and no labeled recordings exist for them yet. Which approach fits first?
options: Retrain a PANNs head each week, waiting until 40 labeled clips per class are collected
Use YAMNet's 521 outputs and map each new insect to the nearest AudioSet class name
Fine-tune AST on AudioSet again
CLAP-style zero-shot: write a prompt per new category and compare text and audio embeddings
blocks.explain: Zero-shot needs only text for each new class, so categories can change at test time. Once labeled clips accumulate, a trained head on embeddings will usually be more accurate and can replace or complement it.

blocks.question: A clip may contain several of your 20 zero-shot classes at once. How should CLAP similarities become per-class decisions?
options: Softmax across the 20 classes and keep only the top one
Apply a sigmoid per class (with a tuned threshold), as the CLAP paper does for multi-label tasks
Use the raw cosine and keep everything above 0
Average all 20 similarities and compare each to the mean
blocks.explain: Softmax forces classes to compete, which suits single-label tasks only. For multi-label data CLAP uses sigmoid per class. Raw cosine above 0 is not a calibrated decision rule.
